title: Jekyll and Hyde: plot and structure
specPoints: Paper 1 Section B: the 19th-century novel, The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
AO2: structure and narrative voice as methods

tips.title: Eight chapters of mystery, two of answers
tips.body: Utterson follows the clues in Chapters 1 to 8; Lanyon and Jekyll explain in 9 and 10.

tips.title: The clues in order
tips.body: The cheque, the will, the stick, the handwriting, the clothes far too large.

tips.title: The door has two faces
tips.body: The neglected door in the by-street is the back of Jekyll's respectable house.

tips.title: Pair the extract with its answer
tips.body: An early extract is answered by Chapter 10; say how the reader rereads it.

tips.title: Who sees what
tips.body: Enfield sees the trampling; a maid sees the murder; Lanyon sees the transformation.

why.matters: The exam prints a passage from the novel and asks about it and the whole book, so the order of chapters and clues has to be yours. The build matters as much as the story: Stevenson withholds his secret through a lawyer who will not ask the obvious question, and hands the answer over in documents at the end. Knowing the build lets an answer place any extract, say what the reader knows at that point, and move out to the chapter that changes its meaning.

examples.title: The detective story you already know
examples.body: Crime novels and television dramas follow the shape Stevenson used: an investigator collects clues the audience sees too, misreads one, and the truth comes in a confession near the end. The pleasure is in the clues, and in seeing afterwards how they fitted.

examples.title: A story told in documents
examples.body: Some novels and podcasts tell a story through letters, diaries, recordings and reports, so the reader assembles the truth like a lawyer. *Jekyll and Hyde* ends that way, and the method makes the reader a judge as well as a listener.

steps.title: A mystery told from outside
steps.body:
Robert Louis Stevenson published *The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde* in 1886. It is a short novel, a novella, in ten chapters, set in London among respectable professional men: a lawyer, two doctors, a butler, a clerk.

**The narrator follows Utterson.** Mr Utterson is a lawyer, “a man of a rugged countenance that was never lighted by a smile” (Chapter 1), reserved, loyal to his friends, and tolerant of their failings: “I incline to Cain’s heresy” (Chapter 1). For eight chapters we see only what he sees, and he does not know the truth.

**The truth comes last, in documents.** The last two chapters are written records: Dr Lanyon's narrative, and Henry Jekyll's full statement of the case. Only there does the reader learn that Jekyll and Hyde are one man.

Most readers now know the secret before they open the book. Stevenson's first readers did not, and the novel is built to keep it from them for as long as possible.

boxes.title: Enfield

check.prompt: Why do the novel's first readers not know that Jekyll and Hyde are the same man until Chapter 9?
check.solution: The third-person narrator stays with Utterson, who is as puzzled as the reader. The secret is held back for Lanyon's narrative and Jekyll's statement. The structure is a mystery's, and the solution comes in writing, after the event.

markScheme.description: The narrator follows Utterson, who does not know, and the truth is kept for the documents in the last two chapters

options: Because Jekyll tells everyone in Chapter 1
The narrator follows Utterson, who does not know, and the truth is kept for the documents in the last two chapters
Because the novel is narrated by Hyde
Because Stevenson did not decide that they were the same man until he had written the first eight chapters, and then changed the ending to surprise his publisher and the readers of the magazine

steps.title: Chapters 1 to 3: a door, a will, a face
steps.body:
**Chapter 1, Story of the Door.** On their Sunday walk Utterson and his cousin Enfield pass a door “equipped with neither bell nor knocker”, “blistered and distained”. Enfield tells what he saw there at three in the morning: a man “trampled calmly over the child’s body and left her screaming on the ground” (Chapter 1); “it was like some damned Juggernaut”. The man paid the child's family close on a hundred pounds, ten in gold and a cheque in a respectable name, and went in by that door. His name is Hyde. “I never saw a man I so disliked” (Chapter 1).

**Chapter 2, Search for Mr Hyde.** Utterson reads Jekyll's will: all his possessions go to Edward Hyde, even if Jekyll simply disappears for three months. Dr Lanyon has fallen out with Jekyll over his science. Utterson watches the door: “I shall be Mr. Seek” (Chapter 2). When he meets Hyde, the man is “Mr. Hyde was pale and dwarfish”, and “if ever I read Satan’s signature upon a face, it is on that of your new friend” (Chapter 2).

**Chapter 3.** At a dinner a fortnight later, Jekyll, “a large, well-made, smooth-faced man of fifty”, asks Utterson to trust him: “the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr. Hyde” (Chapter 3).

rows: A man called Hyde tramples a child
Hyde inherits everything in the will
Hyde, met: dwarfish, hard to describe
Jekyll: I can be rid of him

check.prompt: What does Jekyll's will say, which alarms Utterson in Chapter 2?
check.solution: The will leaves all his possessions to his friend and benefactor Edward Hyde, and adds that Hyde is to inherit if Jekyll disappears or is absent without explanation for over three calendar months. Utterson reads it as a sign that Hyde has a hold over Jekyll; the reader later learns why the clause is there.

markScheme.description: Everything goes to Edward Hyde if Jekyll dies, or disappears for more than three months

options: That Jekyll's house and laboratory are to be given to Dr Lanyon, who is to continue his experiments after his death, and that Utterson is to be paid a large sum to see that this is done
That Hyde is to be arrested if Jekyll dies
Everything goes to Edward Hyde if Jekyll dies, or disappears for more than three months
That Jekyll's money is to go to the hospital

steps.title: Chapters 4 and 5: murder and a letter
steps.body:
**Chapter 4, The Carew Murder Case.** Nearly a year later, in October, a maid at her window sees “an aged beautiful gentleman with white hair” greet a small man in the lane by moonlight. The small man is Hyde, and “with ape-like fury” he beats the old man to death: “the bones were audibly shattered”. The victim is Sir Danvers Carew, a Member of Parliament, carrying a letter addressed to Utterson. The broken stick is one Utterson gave Jekyll years before. Utterson takes the police to Hyde's rooms in Soho, “like a district of some city in a nightmare”. Hyde has gone.

**Chapter 5, Incident of the Letter.** Jekyll, “looking deathly sick”, swears “I swear to God I will never set eyes on him again” (Chapter 5), and shows a letter signed Edward Hyde. Utterson's clerk, Mr Guest, compares it with a note from Jekyll: “the two hands are in many points identical: only differently sloped” (Chapter 5). Utterson's blood runs cold: “Henry Jekyll forge for a murderer” (Chapter 5)!

visuals.alt: A flow chart of Chapters 4 and 5: a maid sees the murder, the stick is Jekyll's, Hyde has gone from Soho, Jekyll swears never again, and the handwriting is the same

check.prompt: What does Utterson conclude when Guest finds the two hands identical except for the slope?
check.solution: He thinks Henry Jekyll forge for a murderer! He reaches the wrong conclusion from the right evidence: the same hand is the truth, but Utterson cannot imagine it. Stevenson lets the reader see a clue that the investigator cannot read.

markScheme.description: That Jekyll has forged a letter for a murderer, to protect him

options: That Guest is lying
That Jekyll and Hyde are the same person
That Hyde has been forging Jekyll's signature on cheques since Chapter 1, which is how he paid the hundred pounds to the child's family, and that Jekyll is innocent of everything
That Jekyll has forged a letter for a murderer, to protect him

steps.title: Chapters 6 to 8: a shock, a window, a door broken
steps.body:
**Chapter 6.** With Hyde gone, Jekyll returns to his friends for two months; then his door is shut again. Lanyon is dying: “I have had a shock” (Chapter 6), and “I wish to see or hear no more of Dr. Jekyll” (Chapter 6). After his death Utterson opens an envelope addressed to him alone and finds inside a sealed enclosure marked “not to be opened till the death or disappearance of Dr. Henry Jekyll”.

**Chapter 7, Incident at the Window.** Utterson and Enfield see Jekyll at a window and speak to him; suddenly his face shows “an expression of such abject terror and despair, as froze the very blood of the two gentlemen below” (Chapter 7), and the window is shut. “God forgive us, God forgive us” (Chapter 7).

**Chapter 8, The Last Night.** Jekyll's butler, Poole, fetches Utterson: he believes his master was made away with eight days ago, and the voice in the cabinet is not his. “that thing was not my master” (Chapter 8). They break down the door with an axe; “A dismal screech, as of mere animal terror”. Inside lies Hyde, “dressed in clothes far too large for him”, dead by poison, “the body of a self-destroyer” (Chapter 8). Jekyll is nowhere. There is a new will naming Utterson, and documents to read.

rows: Lanyon has a shock, and dies
props.title: Chapters 6 to 8

visuals.alt: A table of what happens in Chapters 6, 7 and 8: Lanyon's shock and death, the terror at the window, and the breaking of the door

check.prompt: What do Utterson and Poole find when they break into the cabinet in Chapter 8?
check.solution: The body is Hyde's, in Jekyll's clothes, which are far too big for him, with a crushed phial and the smell of kernels. Utterson calls it the body of a self-destroyer. The clothes are the clue: the reader of the documents will learn why they belong to Jekyll.

markScheme.description: Hyde, dead by poison and dressed in clothes far too large for him, and no sign of Jekyll

options: Hyde, dead by poison and dressed in clothes far too large for him, and no sign of Jekyll
Lanyon, who has been hiding there
Jekyll, alive but very ill, who tells them that Hyde has escaped through the back door into the street and asks them to fetch the police from Scotland Yard at once

steps.title: Chapters 9 and 10: the truth in documents
steps.body: The last two chapters go back in time and tell the story again from inside.

visuals.problem: How do the last two chapters solve the mystery, and in what order?

steps.text: Chapter 9: Lanyon's narrative. Jekyll's letter asked him to fetch a drawer of chemicals and give it at midnight to a messenger. A small man came, mixed the draught, drank it, and changed: “there stood Henry Jekyll”.
steps.note: The fact of the transformation, seen from outside by a man of science. It kills him: my life is shaken to its roots.

steps.text: Chapter 10: Jekyll's statement. He explains why: “man is not truly one, but truly two” (Chapter 10).
steps.note: The reason behind the fact, from inside.

steps.text: He tells how Hyde let him “spring headlong into the sea of liberty”, and how the murder came: “My devil had been long caged, he came out roaring” (Chapter 10).
steps.note: The events of Chapters 1 to 8 retold from the other side.

steps.text: He describes changing without the drug, and the last supply of salt that would not work, because the first had been impure.
steps.note: The reason for the ending: he can no longer come back.

steps.text: He ends before Hyde returns: “I bring the life of that unhappy Henry Jekyll to an end” (Chapter 10).
steps.note: The novel ends on a transformation it never shows.

visuals.alt: A table of the last two chapters: Lanyon's narrative tells what happened, as a witness; Jekyll's statement tells why, from inside

check.prompt: Why does the novel end with Jekyll's statement rather than with the discovery of the body?
check.solution: The body answers what; the statement answers why. Placed last, it makes the reader reread the novel in the mind: the trampling, the will, the letter, the window all change meaning once Jekyll has explained.

markScheme.description: So that the last word is Jekyll's own account of why, which changes how every earlier chapter reads

options: Because Stevenson wanted the police to solve the case in the final chapter, which is why Inspector Newcomen reads Jekyll's statement aloud to Utterson and Poole in the cabinet after the body is found
So that the last word is Jekyll's own account of why, which changes how every earlier chapter reads
Because the body is never discovered
Because Lanyon's narrative is lost

steps.title: Structure as a method: withholding, documents, echoes
steps.body:
Stevenson's structure is the method of a detective story, and the mark scheme for June 2024 named the structure of the novel among the methods an answer might discuss.

**Withholding.** The truth is kept back for eight chapters. The reader, like Utterson, has clues that do not add up: a cheque in a respectable name, a will, a stick, a handwriting.

**Documents.** Letters, a will, an envelope not to be opened, a narrative, a statement. The story is assembled from papers, as a lawyer would assemble a case, and the final truth arrives in writing.

**Echoes.** In Chapter 2 Utterson lies awake and replays Enfield's story: “that human Juggernaut trod the child down”. The June 2024 extract came from that passage, and its indicative content noted Utterson's thoughts echoing events of Chapter 1.

**The door.** The plain door in the by-street is the back of Jekyll's respectable house. Two faces, one building: the geography of the novel is its secret.

steps.title: Writing about narrative structure for AO2
steps.body:
Twelve of the thirty marks are for methods, and the structure of a novel is one of the strongest.

**Name the choice.** Not *there is a twist* but *Stevenson withholds the identity of Jekyll and Hyde for eight chapters by restricting the narrative to Utterson*.

**Say what it does.** The reader shares Utterson's bafflement and feels the fear of what cannot be named; the documents at the end make the reader reread everything.

**Place the extract.** A Chapter 2 extract sits early in the mystery, when Hyde has no face; a Chapter 10 extract is the answer. Say which, and what the reader knows at that point.

**Tie it to an idea.** A story told by respectable men who will not speak of what they suspect is itself about secrecy and reputation.

steps.title: The novel in one page
steps.body:
A lawyer, a door, a will; a murder and a letter; a shock, a window, a door broken; two documents that explain.

- **Chapters 1 to 3:** Enfield's story; the will; Utterson meets Hyde; Jekyll: I can be rid of him.
- **Chapters 4 and 5:** Carew murdered, seen by a maid; the stick; Soho; the letter; the same hand, differently sloped.
- **Chapters 6 to 8:** Lanyon's shock and death; the window; Poole; the door broken; Hyde dead in Jekyll's clothes.
- **Chapter 9:** Lanyon sees Hyde drink the draught and become Jekyll.
- **Chapter 10:** Jekyll's statement: man is truly two; the murder; the impure salt; the end.
- **Structure:** a restricted narrative, withheld truth, documents, echoes, a door with two faces.

questions.prompt: Why does Stevenson restrict the narrative to Utterson for eight chapters?
questions.solution: The restricted view makes a mystery: clues without a solution. Utterson's loyalty and reserve also mean he does not ask the questions the reader wants asked, which deepens the secrecy.

questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph on how Stevenson uses the structure of the novel to create mystery. Refer to at least two structural choices and quote accurately.
questions.solution: Stevenson builds mystery by giving the reader clues and withholding their meaning. For eight chapters the narrative follows Utterson, who sees what a loyal lawyer would see and no more, so the reader collects evidence with him: a cheque in a respectable name, a will that leaves everything to Hyde, a broken stick that Utterson himself gave to Jekyll, and a letter whose hand is “the two hands are in many points identical: only differently sloped”. Utterson reads that last clue wrongly, “Henry Jekyll forge for a murderer”, and the reader, given the right evidence, watches the investigator refuse the truth. The truth then comes in documents, after the event: Lanyon's narrative shows the transformation, “there stood Henry Jekyll”, and Jekyll's statement gives its reason, “man is not truly one, but truly two”. Placed last, the documents make the reader reread the whole novel, so the calm trampling of Chapter 1 becomes a respectable man's hidden pleasure. The structure is also the novel's idea: a story assembled by respectable men who will not say what they suspect is a story about secrecy, and it is told in the manner of the society it describes.

questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph on how Chapter 8, The Last Night, builds tension before the door is broken down.
questions.solution: Chapter 8 is the climax of the mystery, and Stevenson delays the moment of entry so that fear accumulates. Poole's terror comes first: the man who has served Jekyll for twenty years says of the voice in the cabinet, “that thing was not my master”, and calls it a thing, so that the reader hears the unknown before it is seen. Utterson and Poole reason, hesitate and question the evidence, which prolongs the waiting. When the axe falls, the sound from inside is inhuman: “A dismal screech, as of mere animal terror”. The description of what they find is quiet by contrast, Hyde in clothes “dressed in clothes far too large for him”, “the body of a self-destroyer”, and the quiet is more unsettling than the violence. Placed at the end of Utterson's narrative, the chapter solves nothing: Jekyll is missing, and the answer is deferred again to the documents, so the tension is not released but handed on.

questions.prompt: A student writes: "The twist ending is surprising." What is the better account?
questions.solution: Twist names the effect and stops. The structure that produces it, the restricted narrator, the clues, the documents placed last, is what an AO2 answer analyses.

markScheme.description: A restricted narrator withholds the truth and documents reveal it, so the ending makes the reader reread: it is the method

options: A restricted narrator withholds the truth and documents reveal it, so the ending makes the reader reread: it is the method
The ending is not surprising at all, because everybody knows the story, and so the structure has no effect on the reader and cannot be written about for AO2 in the exam
The ending is surprising because Hyde turns out to be Utterson
The novel has no ending

examTechnique.body:
**The extract is a passage; the question is the novel.** Paper 1 Section B prints an extract and asks about it and the novel as a whole.

**Place the extract.** Early chapters are mystery; Chapter 10 is answer. Say what the reader knows at that point.

**Use structure for the whole-text move.** Pair the extract with the chapter that changes its meaning.

**No AO4 on this question.** The 4 AO4 marks on Paper 1 are on the Shakespeare question only.
examinerErrors: Retelling the plot instead of saying what the structure does.
Treating the ending as a twist and stopping there.
Getting the witnesses wrong: a maid sees the murder, Lanyon the transformation.
Forgetting that Utterson is the focus of the narrative for eight chapters.
Staying in the extract and never placing it in the novel.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer knows the novel as a built mystery. It places the extract in the sequence of clues, says what the reader knows and does not know at that point, and moves out to the document that changes the extract's meaning. It names the restricted narrative, the withheld truth and the documents as methods, and ties them to the novel's ideas of secrecy and reputation, with short, exact quotations.
